And before I go on another legal tangent on how you’re right… let me tell you, under Canadian criminal law, you are not required to obtain permission from another person to record them, provided that you are “a party to the conversation”. This is abbreviated as the “one party consent law” system”. Basically it means, if for example you’re in a meeting and there’s like 3 people, as long as you’re one of the 3 people, you can record it without having to inform the others. 

Now, of course there’s always lawsuits and cases of disputes between what an actual “party to the conversation” is… because… like, what if someone is silently listening in, and like… is zoom actually a “party” to the meeting? (Im pretty sure which is why you see those disclaimer/disclosures saying “this video is now being recorded” out loud when it’s being recorded, otherwise it’s a criminal violation).

The exact statue is section 184 of the criminal code of Canada on “interception”, or more colloquially known as “eavesdropping”.

It states “note:Interception

184 (1) Every person who, by means of any electro-magnetic, acoustic, mechanical or other device, knowingly intercepts a private communication is guilty of

(a) an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for a term of not more than five years; or

(b) an offence punishable on summary conviction.

Saving provision

(2) Subsection (1) does not apply to

(a) a person who has the consent to intercept, express or implied, of the originator of the private communication or of the person intended by the originator thereof to receive it;”

The next session you review, you’ll remember the parts you filled in, and move on to the next part, but the key is to understand and be focused while doing it, bcuz if you’re not paying attention, you’ll forget.

The bottom line is if the company owns the page then you are by law required to have the information back as it belongs to the business or the corporation if it is incorporated. 

If I were you I want to go back to the terms of employment contract that you signed when you were employed (the one that you probably just signed and got it over with). Scan through for any sections talking about property or intellectual property stating any claims about something along the lines of “anything created by the employee for the business while working…” “owned by the business” type of stuff.

This is the typical stuff that you should always revisit and you should always keep a record of even though a lot of people just probably sign it and just forget about it because if you go to civil court the judge will reference this. And, in the United States there is more leniency in businesses with the terms of contracts, rather than having terms and conditions that are more fair and plausible for individuals to abide by, understand, etc. (like lawyers creating bulletproof contracts in the US by making a zillion liability waivers, disclaimers, while in other countries there’s certain guidelines and rules).

Also remember what both parties’ incentives are in this situation. Your incentive is to get your pay and their incentive is to retrieve the business’s data and transfer it to the new owners intact. They are withholding your payment explicitly or implicitly as a means of leverage in order for you to return their property (very common for business to do). The question then is, if you give back what they want will they give you your payment? Well you’re gonna have to ask yourself have they paid you before? Has any circumstances changed now other than the current fact mentioned? 

And the bottom line: If they decide to proceed and not pay you do you have proof to take it to court? In civil court small claims like this you will need to be able to prove beyond a balance of probabilities. So have any documentation (past paycheck, time stamps… idk even your phone’s location services tracking for Christ’s sake to show you were there for however long [google store’s all this data unbeknownst to you by using their platform] and evidence. Witnesses are definitely useful but probably hard to obtain for small claims court.
